newsitem.title: UK: UK builders settle dispute, unions call off strike.
newsitem.headline: UK builders settle dispute, unions call off strike.

text.p: A pay deal between construction bosses and unions has headed off a strike by 40,000 British building workers which would have stopped work at key projects and whipped up fears of a summer of industrial action, a union official said on Friday.
Eleventh-hour negotiations late on Thursday produced an agreement which will result in workers getting a 32 percent pay increase over three years.
The talks, held on Thursday in central London, were between the GMB and the Transport and General Workers' unions (T&G) and the Construction Confederation representing the building industry's bosses.

The dispute had threatened to inflame an already-fraught industrial relations climate in Britain this summer after British Airways endured a costly 72-hour strike last week by its cabin crew and headed off a separate conflict with its ground staff.
Royal Mail workers, banking staff at Barclays and London underground crews have also threatened action in the peak summer season and the first disputes under the new Labour government.
Construction workers have not walked out since 1973.

"The negotiations were particularly difficult, but the threat of industrial action concentrated the minds with the eventual conclusion that building workers will be earning on average over 7.50 pounds ($12.54) an hour in 1999," said Allan Black, national officer for the GMB, one of the two unions involved in the dispute.
"This is a deal I can recommend to my members," he said in a statement.

The unions had planned walkouts next month at several projects -- worth hundreds of million of pounds (dollars) -- such as the Channel Tunnel rail link project, the London Underground's Jubilee Line and work on the Millennium Dome, the GMB official said.
"I am particularly pleased that there will be no need for strike action in the construction industry," GMB's Black said.
"No one wanted to embark on such a disruptive course but the negotiations were too drawn out and problematic to allow the employers to continue to drag their heels."
Both sides said they were satisfied that an agreement had been reached over the three years and that any damaging strikes had been averted.

"We're very pleased that a settlement has been reached and the long-term nature of it is very good because it allows companies to have a lot more certainty about their labour costs," said Jenny Price, a spokeswoman for the Construction Confederation.
The dispute with the building employers group flared up at the end of May when the unions rejected as unrealistic management's initial three-year pay deal.
Both unions started a ballot of their members on whether to take strike action last Wednesday.
Union leaders were confident of strong backing for a strike when the ballot results were published next week.
Employers who faced disruptions to key infrastructure projects included Tarmac Plc, Costain Group Plc, John Laing Plc and George Wimpey Plc, the union said. ($ = 0.598 British Pounds)
